item.title: Can Video Games Be a Path to Self-Discovery?
item.description:
Play

Can Video Games Be a Path to Self-Discovery?

A Jungian perspective reveals how video games serve as vessels for creativity.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Video games can be passive fantasy or a form of active imagination.
  • The characters, roles, and play styles one gravitates toward can be the psyche seeking expression.
  • Simple reflective and intentional practices can turn play into a genuine path of self-discovery.
Source: Royce Fonseca / Unsplash

A video game recently began to allow something to open in me. Since I started playing the "World of Warcraft Forever" beta, which I wrote about recently through a Jungian lens, my imagination has been exploding.1 Ideas arrive faster than I can write them down, and powerful internal images keep surfacing in quiet moments. Something dormant within the unconscious seems to have woken up.

Much of this, I think, has to do with playing a mage. Channeling fire and arcane magics through my character became a kind of conduit for what Jung understood as the autonomous nature of the creative impulse: a force that moves through us rather than from us. Each time I cast a spell, I found myself imagining that something deeper was finding expression through the magic, something that wanted form and had been waiting for a vessel.

Jung said as much in his seminar on Nietzsche's Zarathustra: the creative process "creates in us, through us".2 It struck me, too, that Jung saw the magician as one of the guises of spirit; spirit's oldest archetypal images are wind and fire. No wonder the mage felt like such a creative conduit.

That experience has me returning to a question some clients ask in different ways: Is gaming just escape, or can it be something more? The honest answer is that it can be either. What makes the difference isn't the game, but how we show up to play.

Fantasy We Watch vs. Fantasy We Enter

In passive fantasy, images drift past while we watch, and we are entertained but remain psychologically unchanged. Whereas in the Jungian concept of active imagination, we turn toward an image, speak to it, let it respond spontaneously, and we answer back. The conscious "I" steps into the scene and stays there; all sides of us are changed by this creative encounter.

At first glance, video games can look like passive fantasy at its purest: Someone else built the world, and we can sink into it for hours. Yet, games also ask us to act. We make choices and live with the consequences, which is surprisingly close to active imagination. What’s usually missing is the second half: noticing what the encounter stirs in us and allowing something deeper to find expression. When that happens, video games stop being something we consume and become something that creates through us.

When Escape Is Just Escape

It's worth being honest that sometimes we play to numb out, and that isn't a moral failure. Rest is real, and so is the need for relief. There can be a kindness to us in taking it easy for a while. Yet if several days vanish without a trace, or if stopping the game brings existential dread, this deserves curiosity and consideration. The escape may be pointing toward something important in your life. If gaming has become compulsive or obsessive and it’s costing your health, relationships, work, sleep, school grades, or a connection to your inner life, it’s likely worth reaching out to a therapist.

The Avatar as a Vessel

If the creative spirit needs a vessel, the avatar is often the first one we build. Consider the moment of character creation. Who do you become when you're free to become anyone?

Some people always play the healer, keeping everyone else alive. Some reach for the berserker, the trickster, or the lone ranger who never joins a guild. Some play a gender, body, or temperament quite different from the one the world sees in them. These choices are rarely random. In Jungian terms, our characters can embody the shadow, the persona we wish we had, or help us express repressed or emerging identities.

Source: Aleksandra Sapozhnikova / Unsplash

One client of mine, a transgender woman (assigned male at birth), built a character of her authentic gender expression. Inside the game, she could live as herself: be seen, named, heard, and responded to as who she truly is, without the vigilance that daily life demanded. What might look from the outside like fantasy was something closer to sanctuary: a temenos, the protected space in which the Self can begin to take form.3

Rather than continuing to repress and suppress who she is, she had found a vessel through which the Self, the organizing principle of her psyche, could be expressed safely. Her video game sessions gave us a way in to talk about how her authentic inner core was asking to be lived more fully, in the game and beyond it. Sometimes what seeks expression through play is a creative force, and sometimes, as for her, it is the summons of the human soul.4

The point isn’t to diagnose our play style but to get curious about the figures we keep choosing. Video games can be more than an escape and become a genuine doorway into living more creatively and authentically.

Practices for Letting the Creative Spirit Play

  • Set an intention before you play. Not a goal like "reach max level," but a question: What am I looking for tonight? What part of me wants to come out and be expressed?
  • Notice what you choose and what you avoid. The quests you skip and the roles you refuse can be as revealing as the ones you seek.
  • Journal after a session. A few lines are enough: What moved me, what frustrated me, where did I lose track of myself, and what did I learn?
  • Dialogue with your character. Write, draw, and imagine a conversation with your avatar, by hand if you can. Ask what they know that you don't, and what they want from your life outside the game. Let them answer without editing.
  • Let it continue off-screen. Take an image, spell, or landscape from the game and paint, write, or move with it. Let the creative spirit carry it somewhere the game designers never imagined.
  • Bring it home. Ask what the game is asking of you in your actual life. The courage you practise in a raid may want somewhere to go on Monday morning.

Jung saw life itself as the test of spirit: a spirit that pulls us away from life, rather than back into it, is a false one. His cautionary example was Nietzsche, seized by a creative spirit so completely that the man himself was depleted and emptied.1 So, to be authentically inspired is to have spirit breathed into us.

I wonder if you will let something deeper play through you?

item.title: The Mask That Won’t Come Off in "You Can See Everything"
item.description:
Media

The Mask That Won’t Come Off in "You Can See Everything"

Holmes didn’t drop her persona. She simply traded "CEO" for "devoted mom."

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Jung described the "persona" as a mask meant to shape how one is viewed, and to hide one's true nature.
  • Elizabeth Holmes is not actively hiding the truth; she appears to believe the version she projects.
  • Narcissistic distortion can rewrite reality to protect one's ego, which may explain Holmes' lack of remorse.
"You Can See Everything's" Elizabeth Holmes
Source: A24

You Can See Everything is a captivating and brilliant documentary from comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim that turns the lens on Elizabeth Holmes and her family for 34 days before she goes to prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and lying to investors and consumers about the capabilities of her blood analyzers. The A24 documentary You Can See Everything has been one of the strongest openings in 20 years. This film has everyone talking and wondering who the real Elizabeth Holmes is, yet many of us are still left feeling as if we saw everything but the truth.

Elizabeth Holmes is still Elizabeth Holmes. She’s just swapped one persona for another. Because Holmes believes her own version of the truth, she is so convincing that even the filmmakers and the audiences can’t seem to figure out what is real and what is not.

The word persona comes from the Latin word for masks worn by actors in ancient theater. The mask, or persona, resembles the person, but is partly created by society. For instance, when you come home from work, you might leave your work persona at the door and become a more intimate or real version of yourself behind closed doors. In Carl Jung's Collected Works Vol. 7, the persona is described as “a complicated system of relations between the individual consciousness and society, fittingly enough a kind of mask, designed on the one hand to make a definite impression upon others, and, on the other, to conceal the true nature of the individual.”

In the documentary, the black turtleneck-wearing, deep, masculinized-voiced CEO persona of Elizabeth Holmes that we all know so well from TED Talks, magazine covers, and the Hulu series “The Dropout” is replaced by a tan, crewneck-sweater-wearing, softer, higher-pitched-voiced mother and wife. This new persona serves to authenticate what Elizabeth Holmes wants us to know: that she did not do anything wrong. Theranos “could” work, and she has nothing to hide. What she wants us to see is authenticity, but we may be looking at narcissistic distortion.

As psychotherapist Erin Leonard writes, “Narcissists live and die by their own version of the truth. Is it the truth if reality has been distorted? A narcissist believes it is.” Holmes is rewriting reality to protect her fragile ego, which is why we never really see remorse for her wrongdoing. The persona of Holmes isn't dropped; we aren’t seeing the real her, but we are seeing another reality, and the primary reality is absent.

Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes, Nathan Fielder
Source: A24

Nathan Fielder challenges the way we see documentaries and the cinéma vérité genre, in which the filmmaker remains just a “fly on the wall.” Instead, Fielder inserts himself as a main character, challenging and questioning Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at every step. However, he does not do this from a journalistic perspective or even as someone who understands engineering, but as someone like us—someone who just wants Holmes to say, “I messed up. I lied because I did not want to fail.”

But the confession, the remorse, or "the magic trick revealed" never happens. Instead, you get a portrait of a woman who has reconstructed her image to appeal to us, once again, as someone we should trust. In this version, her husband helps. He tells us she “thinks differently” from other people and that we should believe what we see.

In some ways, he is right, just not in the way he is insinuating. Neurodivergents think differently than someone who is non-neurodivergent, and individuals who are narcissistic think differently from those who are not. Fielder is quick to want to teach Holmes how magic tricks work, but as smart as Holmes is, she never quite seems to get his metaphors or his jokes as they apply to her.

"You Can See Everything"
Source: A24

The ultimate magic of the film is that we think we are going behind closed doors to see an unmasked version of Holmes, but what we find is someone whose mask does not (or cannot) come off. She is, and believes herself to be, exactly the persona she is projecting to us. That is why we feel so uneasy when we hear her say, "I have nothing to hide." If Fielder even gets close to something—a glimmer of remorse or authentic vulnerability—her husband conveniently interrupts or shuts down the cameras—not to protect the person, but the persona. Holmes is not hiding some truth we need to discover; she is living a version of her truth, and that's what makes it impossible for us to ever really see everything.

item.title: The Many Sides of Living With Former Search-and-Rescue Dogs
item.description:
Animal Behavior

The Many Sides of Living With Former Search-and-Rescue Dogs

Tracy Darling tells us about former search-and-rescue dogs and what they need.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Search-and-rescue dogs are caught in a double bind: they love to work but far too often get a bad rap.
  • High-drive dogs are often placed into lives that have little to offer them, so they are not really failures.
  • Tracy Darling helps people see the love and magic in these dogs, their intensity, curiosity, and drive.
High-drive dog, Beth, now an active family companion, is always ready for a game of fetch.
Source: Search Dog Foundation, used with permission

Search-and-rescue (SAR) dogs are highly unique canines. For 30 years, the National Disaster Search Dog Foundation has looked for potential in a place many people overlook: the shelter system. They seek highly driven dogs: intense, persistent, curious animals often described as too energetic, too busy, or too much. Yet the traits that prevented success in one placement can make a dog extraordinary in the right one.

Disaster search is elite work, and not every dog they recruit will be suited to it. When a dog does not make that narrow grade, their responsibility shifts to finding a life where that dog can thrive. That experience motivates them to help more people see the magic in these dogs: the possibility hidden inside all that intensity, curiosity, and drive.

Here's what Tracy Darling, Senior Director of Canine Operations at the National Disaster Search Dog Foundation, says about retired life for high-drive dogs.

Marc Bekoff: How did you get interested in this work, and what did you learn about shelter dogs that you did not expect?

Tracy Darling: I was first drawn to this work by images from the aftermath of September 11: dogs and handlers moving through rubble, accomplishing something no machine could. The work was heroic, but actually living with a high-drive dog changed my understanding of the story. I thought we were teaching dogs to do remarkable things. Instead, they were teaching us to live differently. They required clearer communication and greater presence.

The bigger surprise was where these dogs came from. Repeatedly, the dog with the most potential was one who had already been returned once or twice. Those dogs had not failed. They had been placed into lives that had little to offer them.

MB: Why do high-drive dogs get a bad rap? What are the most common misconceptions?

TD: The most common misconception is that drive is a behavior problem. It is not. Drive is a strong internal need to engage with the world: to move, play, explore, solve problems, and work toward something with a partner. Trouble begins when that drive has no direction. A dog with significant capacity and nothing meaningful to do will invent an outlet...then come the labels: hyper, destructive, reactive, stubborn, impossible.

Another misconception is that an intense dog cannot also be sensitive. Dogs who throw themselves wholeheartedly into life often bring that same commitment to relationships. The dog who notices every shift in the environment may also be finely tuned to the person holding the leash. Their intensity does not make them less connected. Often, it means they are taking in more, reacting more fully, and investing more deeply in the world around them.

MB: What kind of home does a dog like this thrive in? Are there personality patterns, or the same range seen in other dogs?

TD: Drive describes how strongly a dog wants to participate, not the dog's entire personality. High-drive dogs may be outgoing or reserved, socially flexible or selective, bold or slower to settle into new situations. The right home is therefore less about a checklist than a rhythm. It includes the dog rather than managing life around the dog. There is room to move, something to learn, and a person who enjoys being part of the process.

That does not mean nonstop activity. Rest is a skill, too, and a thoughtful home has space for quiet after the dog's needs have been met. What rarely works is asking the dog to become a background character. If the dog's daily experience is watching life from the other side of a window, training alone will not solve the mismatch.

MB: What does training look like for a dog whose defining trait is that they want to work?

TD: For these dogs, development is less about formal training than about the opportunities daily life provides. A driven dog wants to learn, move, solve problems, and work with a partner. Those are not rewards offered after the real work. They are the work: a trail walk before the day begins, a game of fetch that becomes a shared ritual, a training session that challenges both partners.

When those opportunities are present, many behaviors become easier because the dog is no longer carrying so much unspent capacity. Our approach emphasizes shared joy, collaboration, and clear communication because high-drive dogs aren’t interested in complying with a list of rules. They are looking for meaningful engagement. The strongest partnerships are built when the dog wants to participate, not when the dog is simply managed into obedience.

MB: What happens to the dogs who do not make the grade for disaster search, and what have those placements taught you?

TD: They go on to active, well-matched lives, and we remain involved in their success. Some find purpose in detection work or dog sports where intensity is an asset. Many become exceptional companions for active people: hiking partners, running buddies, weekend co-pilots, and daily reminders to get outside, stay curious, and do more together.

Not making the grade for disaster search is not a judgment on the dog. It reflects an extremely specialized selection process. A dog can be exceptional and still not belong on a rubble pile. These placements remind us that fit is more powerful than perfection. The same dog who overwhelms one household may feel easy, joyful, and deeply rewarding in another. The dog did not change; the context did. In the right life, curiosity becomes adventure, persistence becomes determination, intensity becomes enthusiasm, and drive becomes connection.

MB: What would you say to someone considering a dog like this?

TD: The most useful question may not be, “Can I handle this dog?” but, “What might this dog open up in my life?” A high-drive dog may invite you outside earlier, take you farther, and draw you into new skills, new places, and new communities. They can turn an ordinary walk into a shared project, a training session into a conversation, and daily life into something more active, connected, and alive.

The relationship is not effortless, and that is part of its value. It is built through thousands of small moments: noticing, communicating, trying again, celebrating progress. These dogs ask you to participate. They ask for clarity, curiosity, and a willingness to build a life with them rather than simply make room for them. In return, they often expand the lives of the people who choose them. Some dogs fit comfortably into the life already there. Others invite that life to become bigger. The dogs who want more are everywhere, waiting for someone to see that what looks like too much may be exactly the beginning of something extraordinary.

item.title: How to Curb Your Vices
item.description:
Rationalization

How to Curb Your Vices

Knowing when to seek help for habits that are hard to break.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Vices are always in the eyes of the beholder and are learned ways of coping with stress.
  • The keys to putting the brakes on them is to track your triggers and have healthier substitute behaviors.
  • If underlying depression or anxiety is present, get professional support.
Source: max60500/Pixabay

We’re not talking about addictions here, where both habit and brain physiology can take control of your life. Instead, we’re talking about vices, those breakout behaviors that are always in the eyes of the beholder, your personal list of no-nos and shouldn’ts—too much sugar, alcohol, or food, shopping therapy, porn bingeing, or sexual acting out. Behaviors that periodically flare up, that you know aren't the best, and that, while they create a tinge of guilt, never generate enough guilt to overcome those hefty doses of rationalization.

We can think of vices as bad solutions to underlying problems. Here are some of the most common ones.

Stress

Worry, exhaustion, frustration, anger—some negative emotional state. Your vice gives you the dopamine hit you’ve learned counteracts stress. Rationalization adds its own fuel to the mix—you feel you deserve to do whatever you’re doing.

Life out of balance

For some, their vices are a byproduct of an unbalanced lifestyle. Here we meet those who believe in working hard, often pushing themselves to exhaustion, and then playing hard—the kicking back they, like the others, feel they deserve.

Putting the brakes on your behavior

But if you’re concerned about behaviors because of their side effects, whether financial, relational, or simply the regret afterward, or if you worry you’ve been relying on them too much, it may be time to put the brakes on. Here are some tips:

Know your triggers; take your emotional pulse. Does the refrigerator, liquor cabinet, or computer call to you the moment you walk through the door after a hard day at work? Good to know. If you’re tired, worried, or feeling the urge to kick back, you’re likely vulnerable to bad behaviors.

The key is checking in with yourself—taking your emotional pulse—before you hit that front door. Once triggers kick in, you run on autopilot.

Have substitute behaviors at the ready. Putting on the brakes doesn’t mean white-knuckling it; instead, it means substituting other behaviors that can reduce your stress. For some, it might be exercise to boost your endorphins; for others, it may be self-care such as a hot bath, talking to a friend, or listening to your favorite music; for still others, it may help to write down how you’re feeling or thinking just to get it out of your head.

Make a list of these options and keep it handy so you don’t have to reinvent the wheel or scramble every time these temptations flare up. Decide what you’re going to do before you hit the front door.

Consider seeking professional help

If these patterns are increasingly taking control of your daily life, you may need additional support. Even short-term therapy can help you develop skills to manage your stress or lifestyle more effectively. You may have underlying depression and/or anxiety that can benefit from medication and therapy.

The antidote is action: Is it time to hit the brakes?

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: An Archetype Guide for Elders
item.description:
Wisdom

An Archetype Guide for Elders

Some archetypes stay with us for life; others arrive during our last act.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • A goddess is a mythological figure, while an archetype is the universal energy she represents.
  • Goddess myths are ancient stories, but their patterns live within human beings.
  • Recognizing one's inner goddesses helps people understand themselves.

Once a month in my town, I offer a Sacred Circle for women 60 and over. Our themed discussions are rich as elders share their wisdom.

This month’s theme, "The Feminine Archetypes," focused on the stage Jean Shindola Bolen calls "the juicy crone," although I prefer the gentler word, "elders."

Words to know:

  • Goddess: a female divine being in mythology or religion
  • Archetype: a universal pattern or character found in stories across cultures
  • Myth: an ancient story that carries a truth about human life
  • Crone: an older word for a wise elder woman, reclaimed today as a title of honor

Archetypes honor our lived experiences, and invite us to examine the archetypes, past and present, within us.

By elderhood, many of us have typically reached the place of "self-acceptance," the ability to say, "This is who I am." The late Gloria Steinem observed that women get more radical with age—more knowing and fierce.

What Are Archetypes?

Archetypes are universal patterns of energy and character that appear in myths, dreams, and lives across cultures. We each carry many. Some have shaped our lives for decades; others have been waiting to emerge in our latter years.

Think of archetypes as seeds that are in all of us from the beginning. Depending upon circumstance and predisposition, some become activated and others remain dormant. (Bolen, p. 203).

Why Study Archetypes?

Understanding archetypes can help us become more conscious of our potential age; activating them can energize us and help us find new meaning. Many think of this third act of life (beginning at 60) as a time of wholeness and integration.

Seven Feminine Archetypes

Over our lifetime, we move through seven feminine archetypes. These are fluid internal patterns, and most of us embody more than one: a primary energy plus two or three secondary ones.

  1. The Maiden (Persephone): driven by beginnings and possibilities
  2. The Lover (Aphrodite): driven by sensuality and creative expression
  3. Huntress (Artemis): driven by autonomy and independence
  4. The Mother (Demeter): driven by a desire to nurture and protect
  5. The Mystic (Hestia): driven by inner peace and solitude; spiritually centered
  6. The Sage (Athena): driven by clarity; desire to mentor
  7. The Queen (Hera): driven by leadership and a legacy

Goddesses Who Grow Old With Us

Each of these goddesses was probably part of our younger lives. She doesn't leave as we age; she ripens.

Demeter: Greek goddess of the harvest, the Mother

  • Earlier in life: the nurturer, the provider
  • In later life: nurturing grandchildren, friends, community, and the earth
  • You may know her when you feed people, garden, or volunteer.

Hestia: Greek goddess of hearth and home, the Mystic

  • Earlier in life: the woman who needs quiet time alone
  • In later life: contemplation, prayer, meditation, a calm inner center
  • You may know her when you savor your morning tea in silence.

Athena: Greek goddess of wisdom, the Sage

  • Earlier in life: the planner and achiever
  • In later life: seasoned judgment and the desire to mentor
  • You may know her when friends call you for clear-headed advice.

Hera: the Queen

  • Earlier in life: leadership and legacy-building.
  • In later life: ruling her own life and making choices without asking permission
  • You may know her when you say "no" without apologizing.

Goddesses Who Emerge in Later Life

These goddesses often arrive bringing four gifts: wisdom, compassion, fierceness, and humor.

The Gift of Wisdom

Metis, Greek goddess of practical wisdom

  • Who she was: Athena's mother, swallowed by Zeus, and her wisdom lived inside him.
  • What she offers: practical, instinctive know-how.
  • You may know her when you solve a problem no one else could or realize how often your wisdom went uncredited.

Sophia, wisdom in feminine form, honored in Jewish and Christian traditions

  • What she offers: spiritual wisdom; a sense of what’s sacred and what gives life meaning.
  • You may know her when you sense a larger purpose or pattern in your life story.

Hecate, Greek goddess of crossroads and intuition

  • Who she was: guardian of thresholds, who carried her torch to help Demeter search for Persephone.
  • What she offers: intuition and guidance through life's transitions.
  • You may know her when you face retirement, a move, or a loss, and trust your inner knowing.

The Gift of Compassion

Quan Yin, Chinese Buddhist goddess of mercy

  • Who she is: her name means "one who hears the cries of the world."
  • What she offers: mercy toward others and ourselves.
  • You may know her when you forgive yourself for something you've carried for years.

The Gift of Fierceness

Sekhmet, destroyer who was also a healer

  • Who she was: a lioness whose fury could destroy, and who was also a goddess of healing.
  • What she offers: righteous anger and the courage to protect what matters.
  • You may know her when you speak up about an injustice, or stop being "nice" when nice isn't right.

The Gift of Humor

Baubo, from Demeter's story

  • Who she was: an earthy old woman whose bawdy jokes made the grieving Demeter laugh.
  • What she offers: healing laughter and a refusal to take life too seriously.
  • You may know her when you laugh at yourself, or at the absurdities of aging.

The Crone or Elder Archetype

This is a soul-satisfying time. Margaret Mead called this the PMZ: post-menopausal zest. The crone phase is about inner development, not outer appearance. An elder woman truly knows who she is.

It is also called a "choicemaker" when women do what is true for them at a soul level. We have found our voice. To be a crone means letting go of what should have been, could have been, or might have been.

According to Bolen, to flourish in this stage of our lives, we must release past resentments and disappointments, and stop seeing ourselves as victims of our past.

The Crone invites us to reflect on what we’ve learned. We value compassion and decisiveness, but we also know we can be fierce when needed: Gloria Steinem fierce!

Crones do not turn away from reality. They see flaws in themselves and others, but without harsh judgment; they have learned to trust themselves.

Angeles Arrien (2013), anthropologist, author, and crone, offers four guiding principles for this stage:

  1. Show up.
  2. Pay attention.
  3. Speak your truth.
  4. Don’t be attached to outcome.

In later life, women can draw on a rich inner cast of feminine archetypes. Some, like Demeter, Hestia, Athena, and Hera, grow old with us and ripen. Others, like Metis, Hecate, Quan Yin, Sekhmet, and Baubo, often appear only with age, bringing wisdom, compassion, fierceness, and humor. Together they point to the Crone: an elder who knows who she is, lets go of old resentments, and speaks her truth.

item.title: Pay Attention to Your Attention
item.description:
Attention

Pay Attention to Your Attention

The fitness revolution taught us to train our bodies. Now let's train our minds.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Since the 1960s, deliberate care for our bodies has become routine for many people.
  • Attensity!, calls for a cultural awakening about where we place our attention.
  • Small daily habits, practiced individually and together, can help us reclaim our attention.

We make appointments to exercise. We arrange our schedules around a jog, a yoga class, or a trip to the gym. For many of us, caring for our bodies has become a routine part of our week. We understand that physical well-being deserves deliberate attention. But we weren’t always this aware.

In the early 1960s, intentional exercise occupied a very different place in American life. Yet the now-familiar expectation that adults would schedule regular workouts was much less established. In December 1960, President-elect John F. Kennedy published “The Soft American” in Sports Illustrated, urging greater concern for physical fitness. As president, he made fitness a national priority, and the shift accelerated.

Over the following decades, health clubs and organized exercise became familiar features of daily life. Jim Fixx, Jane Fonda, Jack LaLanne, Richard Simmons, and Arnold Schwarzenegger inspired millions to get off the couch and start moving.

Gradually, we learned to pay attention to our bodies. We noticed the consequences of inactivity. We made room for movement. Communities and businesses created places to exercise, and friends encouraged one another to participate.

The change was cultural as well as personal. Taking time to care for the body became understandable, acceptable, and, for many, expected. It also became a multibillion-dollar business.

Attensity! A Manifesto of the Attention Liberation Movement discusses this cultural revolution and foresees a similar transformation. Its authors make a bold prediction: “Attentional wellness—the training and conditioning and maintenance of one’s diverse attentional capacities—will, in 2040, be understood as a basic good; simply pragmatic on the one hand (because one is more effective in the world when one’s attention is healthy and well), but also more than merely ‘useful’ since attentional wellness is also beautiful (it brings joy, and makes for richer lives, deeper intimacies, and a better world).”

The Friends of Attention, the collective behind this 2026 book, invite us to consider a cultural change: becoming conscious of where our attention goes and reclaiming a say in its direction. They urge us to make deliberate care for our attention as familiar as working out has become for our bodies.

Who is choosing what receives your attention?

Social media makes that question especially pressing. Its recommendations continually offer something else to watch, read, or react to. The Friends of Attention have a vivid name for this: “human fracking.” Just as drilling companies extract oil and gas from the earth, they argue, technology companies extract our attention and sell it. AI adds another layer: We can ask a system to select information, summarize an experience, or generate a response before we’ve considered what we think ourselves.

I remain enthusiastic about technology. A thoughtful exchange online, an illuminating article, or a useful AI conversation can deserve our attention. The point of the fracking metaphor is not that technology is bad, but that our attention is valuable—valuable enough that others are working hard to capture it. The question is whether we are choosing those encounters consciously and noticing how they are affecting us.

Dr. Jessica Kizorek, at Florida International University, shared, “My students are slowly beginning to recognize how easily AI can hijack their emotional and intellectual attention. In my class, we talk about the ‘rabbit hole’ as an experience that can be driven by their own curiosity or by AI sucking them in without their conscious attention.”

Just as early research on inactivity helped spark the fitness movement, new research suggests that unexamined attention carries costs, too. A 2025 survey of 319 knowledge workers by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon researchers found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less self-reported critical thinking in AI-assisted tasks.

A 2025 randomized study in PNAS Nexus found that blocking mobile internet on smartphones for just two weeks improved sustained attention, subjective well-being, and mental health. Our attention, it seems, responds quickly when our environment changes.

Begin by noticing

The manifesto leaves us with a question we can carry into everyday life: What am I giving my attention to, and how is it affecting me?

Try pausing at a few ordinary moments. Before opening an app, ask what you came to do. After using it, notice whether you did that. During a conversation, observe whether you are listening or preparing your reply. If you find yourself deep in a rabbit hole, borrow the question Dr. Kizorek gives her students: "Am I directing this exploration, or is AI directing me?" These pauses can reveal choices we otherwise miss.

Then consider what you would like to give more of your attention to. Perhaps it is your partner, a book, music, your neighborhood, or your own thoughts. Choose one and make room for it today.

There is no need to make every moment goal-oriented. Watching clouds, enjoying a silly conversation, or lingering over a painting can be deeply worthwhile. We can allow our attention to be playful, receptive, and unhurried.

A change we can make together

The fitness revolution thrived on collective action. A culture of attention needs that too. Families can agree to put phones aside during meals. Friends can take walks together. Schools can create space for sustained discussion, and workplaces can protect periods without an expectation of immediate replies.

Clinicians can invite reflection: Where does your attention go during a typical day? Where would you like it to go? What would make that easier?

In 1960, Kennedy worried that Americans were growing soft. Today the risk is a different kind of softness: attention that goes wherever it is pulled. We learned to build strength, endurance, and flexibility in our bodies. We can build them in our minds, too.

This manifesto caught my attention; I hope it catches yours.

The first exercise takes no equipment, and you can start it now: Pay attention to your attention.

item.title: The Surprising Psychological Benefits of Letter Writing
item.description:
Relationships

The Surprising Psychological Benefits of Letter Writing

Handwritten letters help us deepen relationships and improve our mental health.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Only around one-third of Americans have sent handwritten letters in the past year.
  • Letter writing can help deepen relationships through shared vulnerability and intimacy.
  • Most people love receiving letters and report feeling closer to the sender as a result.
Source: Sue Hughes/Unsplash

Less than one-third of Americans have written and sent an old-fashioned letter in the last year. I’m talking about taking out the stationery, writing “Dear So-and-So,” licking the envelope, putting a stamp in the corner, and placing it in the mailbox with the little red flag proudly raised.

I know I'm not the only one, but I took up letter writing this fall after reading (and falling in love with) Virginia Evans’s novel, The Correspondent. It features a less-than-perfect older protagonist who writes all sorts of correspondence for all sorts of reasons. I loved getting to know this woman through her letters and started wondering what legacy I will leave with only digital traces of my thoughts, feelings, and ideas.

So I drove to the local stationery store and purchased the fanciest stationery and most luxurious envelopes. I also bought a physical address book and started collecting mailing addresses of friends and family past and present. Then, I carved out a little time every week to think deeply about whoever I was writing to and create and send the most personalized notes I could.

Letter writing has some powerful benefits that we just can’t get from sending a text or an email.

Writing Letters Allows Us to Share Deeper Thoughts and Feelings

According to Sara Algoe, a professor in the psychology and neuroscience department at the University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill, relationships are built on self-disclosure. When we reveal our deeper thoughts, feelings, and ideas, we connect with others through shared intimacy, a shared intimacy of revelations and disclosures that is much less likely when we’re communicating through the internet or even in person.

When I’m writing a letter, I find myself contemplating what I will say next and using my words carefully in a way that I don’t when I talk to people face-to-face.

People Love Receiving Letters

I have been blown away by the response to my letters. People have sent strings of joyful and revealing texts, scheduled FaceTime meetings with me, and even been inspired to visit me, all because of my letters.

According to a Gallup poll, over 94% of respondents feel positive about receiving personal letters. People feel good about getting personal letters in the mail, more so than birthday cards and packages. Knowing someone went out of their way to gather the supplies, reflect on our relationship, and put those thoughts down on paper means more than receiving yet another hurried text.

Letter Writing Helps Us Focus on Gratitude

There are tons of studies showing how impactful practicing gratitude can be, especially expressing what we’re grateful for in writing. Expressing our gratitude in writing can help lower stress and improve sleep quality.

Make sure to slip in some gratitude into your letters to experience some of these physical benefits. Reflect on what you appreciate, adore, and admire in whoever you’re writing to.

Join Me: Write a Letter

It’s been about two months, and I have yet to receive any letters in response to my initial correspondence. The wild thing is that it doesn’t bother me at all. I’m not writing letters to get letters. I’m writing letters to bolster friendships and relationships old and new. I’m writing letters to reflect on what I’m grateful for, to meditate, to think on the page. I’m writing letters to make other people’s days. Imagining my beautiful stationery being read by someone I love is gift enough.

So join me. Go out and get some stationery and some stamps, and let's get to writing.
